Tosafot on Bava Batra 101a:1:1.hebrew: ורחבן ששה - ואפי' למ"ד בסוכה (דף ח.) שהאדם תופס אמה, היינו כשהוא לבוש; אבל מת שאינו לבוש כל כך, אף עם הארון לא הוי כי אם אמה. ותדע, דבלא מלבוש אין מחזיק אמה, דהא מקוה אינו אלא אמה על אמה ברום ג' אמות, ואי אדם ערום מחזיק אמה אמה באמתא היכי יתיב:
Tosafot on Bava Batra 101a:1:1.english: And their width is six - Even according to the one who says in Sukkah (8a) that a person occupies a cubit, that is when he is clothed. But a dead person, who is not so clothed, even with the coffin, would take up only a cubit. And you can know this, for without clothing he does not occupy a cubit, since a *mikveh* is only one cubit by one cubit with a height of three cubits, and if a naked person occupied a cubit by a cubit, how could he sit in a cubit-by-cubit space?

Tosafot on Bava Batra 101a:3:1.hebrew: ועושה חצר על פתח המערה - כאן משמע שהחצר גבוהה מן המערה, דהא בעי למימר בגמרא שאחד מימין הפתח ואחד משמאל נכנסין לתוך החצר, דקאמר בגמרא: "אי לבראי, הא קא מיתדשי". וקשה, דבפרק משוח מלחמה (סוטה דף מד.) משמע שאין החצר שוה עם קרקע עולם אלא עמוקה, וצריך לעלות כשיוצא ממנו, דמפליג בין פתחה למעלה לפתחה מן הצד. וכן פירוש רש"י שם. ויש לומר: דאף על פי שהחצר עמוקה, המערה עמוקה הימנה:
Tosafot on Bava Batra 101a:3:1.english: "And he makes a courtyard at the opening of the cave" - Here it implies that the courtyard is higher than the cave, for the Gemara wants to say that one [cave] to the right of the opening and one to the left enter into the courtyard, as the Gemara says: "If [they open] outward, they will be trampled." But this is difficult, for in the chapter of Meshuach Milchamah (Sotah 44a) it implies that the courtyard is not level with the ground but is sunken, and one must climb up when exiting from it, as [the Gemara] distinguishes between its opening being above and its opening being at the side. And so too is Rashi's explanation there. And one can answer: Even though the courtyard is sunken, the cave is deeper than it.

Tosafot on Bava Batra 101a:6:1.hebrew: אי לבראי הא קא מיתדשי - ה"ה דה"מ למיפרך הא קא נגעי אהדדי, אלא אומר ר"ת: משום דה"מ לשנויי במעמיק כדמשני בסמוך, ועדיפא מיניה פריך:
Tosafot on Bava Batra 101a:6:1.english: "If [they throw them] outside, they will be trampled" - The same [reasoning] applies, as [the Gemara] could have asked: "But they are touching one another!" Rather, Rabbeinu Tam says: [The Gemara did not ask this] because [the one answering] could have answered by [saying that he digs] deeply, as [the Gemara] answers shortly afterward; and so it asks a better question than that.

Tosafot on Bava Batra 101a:6:2.hebrew: ותו התנן חצר הקבר העומד בתוכה טהור - וא"ת לר"ש, היכי אזיל? כיון שיש ד' מערות לד' רוחות. וכי תימא באמה שבין כוך לכוך — האמר בפרק משוח מלחמה (שם) דמת תופס ארבע אמות היכא דלא מסיימי מחיצות, ודוקא בחצר הוא דמסיימי מחיצות אינו תופס. ופ"ה דאזיל שם בשידה תיבה ומגדל:
Tosafot on Bava Batra 101a:6:2.english: And furthermore, did we not learn: "The courtyard of the grave; one who stands inside it is pure" - And if you ask: according to R. Shimon, how does [the one who enters] walk there, since there are four caves on the four sides? And if you say [he walks] in the cubit between one burial niche and the next — but did it not say in the chapter Meshuach Milchamah (there) that a corpse occupies four cubits where the partitions are not defined, and it is specifically in a courtyard, where the partitions are defined, that it does not occupy [four cubits]? And Rashi explains that he walks there in a shidah, teivah, or migdal [that is, an enclosed vessel or structure that shields against impurity].

Tosafot on Bava Batra 101a:7:1.english: That he made them like a nagar - This is puzzling. Even so, why is the one standing inside it pure? Surely a corpse takes up four cubits, since the partitions are not complete, because the corpse is buried within the courtyard itself. If we said that the wall of the cave is a cubit [thick], it would work well. But that is not implied below, where [the Mishnah] counts twenty-two according to R. Shimon and eighteen according to the Rabbis, which implies that there is nothing at all between the hollow of the cave and the courtyard. And if you say that he returns a partition around the corpse, then it would not be a six-by-six courtyard, and much would be missing from it, since there are eight corpses for the four openings of the courtyard that open onto the four caves. [Furthermore,] Rabbenu Yitzchak (Ri) found it difficult: how can it be that the opening of the cave is only two cubits wide, and how would they enter with the corpse? For necessarily it contains nothing more than a kokh made like a nagar, one cubit by one cubit wide. And if so, each kokh must be kept a cubit away from the corner, for otherwise it is impossible that the eight kokhim in the courtyard would not touch one another. So for two kokhim there are two cubits, plus the cubit that he leaves at each corner, and only two cubits remain for the opening. (1) And Rashba says that the opening can be three cubits wide. For example, he can always keep the kokh to the right of the opening a cubit away, and make the one on the left in the corner. That is three cubits for the two kokhim together with the gap, which leaves three cubits for the opening. (2) The kokh on the left is right in the corner, and is only half a cubit away from the one placed lengthwise in the cave, lying down. But one need not be strict about this, since this one is made like a nagar and is only a cubit by a cubit wide. We are indeed strict about the one lying across the width of the cave, to keep it half a cubit from the corner. The one lying along the length of the cave is likewise half a cubit from the corner, and it keeps moving away evenly toward the south, while the one placed across the width of the cave keeps moving away evenly toward the east, so they come close together only at their heads. Nevertheless, the Sages did not distinguish among those lying down. And further, one can give a reason: even if they had not kept the one lying across the width of the cave half a cubit from the corner, they would have gained nothing. They could not have reduced the width of the cave by a cubit on that account and shortened it, since then its width would be five, and this cannot be according to R. Shimon, because of those kokhim on the side of the opening, on the right and on the left. According to the Rabbis too, where there are no kokhim by the opening, they could not have made its width less than four, for otherwise how would they bring in the coffin, which is four cubits, into the kokh that runs along the length of the cave? And even now that the cave is four [cubits] wide, it is difficult: how does a cubit sit within a cubit? Rather, its width was not exactly four, but slightly more than four cubits. And there is another way to explain: at the very least the opening is two and a half cubits wide, with the one on the right a cubit from the corner and the one on the left half a cubit. (3) This is also how it appears to Ri. And one must examine how they descended from the courtyard to the cave. If the courtyard sloped downward at the place where one enters the four caves on its four sides, then it would not have been fit to use the lower part and its burial places. Rather, certainly the courtyard was an even six by six, and they descended from the courtyard to the cave by a ladder, or there were slopes from the courtyard to the cave:

Tosafot on Bava Batra 101a:7:2.hebrew: דעביד להו כמין נגר - והא דתנן בסוף נזיר (דף סד:): "המוצא מת מושכב כדרכו", ואמר בגמרא: "מושכב" — פרט ליושב. לר' יוסי בר' חנינא דהכא, דוקא יושב ממעט ולא עומד:
Tosafot on Bava Batra 101a:7:2.english: That he makes them like a bar - And as for what we learned at the end of Nazir (64b): "One who finds a corpse lying in its usual manner," and the Gemara says: "Lying" — this excludes one sitting. According to R. Yose b. R. Hanina here, only sitting is excluded, but not standing.
